opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really useful distinction to make. With Genie, there are basically two separate questions: what changed between frames, and how do you actually render the next frame given that change.

The "what it predicts" part comes from the latent action model. We train Genie on internet videos, mostly 2D platformer gameplay, and those videos don't come with any action labels. Nobody tells you which button the player pressed. So we learn a small discrete set of latent actions in an unsupervised way. The model looks at a frame and the frame after it and asks: what's the minimal piece of information that explains the transition? We deliberately keep that bottleneck tiny, something like eight possible actions. That forces the model to capture the controllable part of the change, like the character moving left, moving right, or jumping, rather than everything going on in the scene.

The "how it generates" part is the dynamics model. It's an autoregressive transformer that works over video tokens from our tokenizer. It takes the history of tokenized frames plus a latent action and predicts the tokens for the next frame. So the dynamics model handles the detail: what the background looks like, how the parallax scrolls, how the character's sprite looks mid-jump. The action just tells it which way to go.

At inference time you drop the part of the latent action model that looks at the future frame. A user, or eventually an agent, picks one of those discrete actions, and the dynamics model rolls the world forward. That separation is what makes Genie feel playable. You get consistent controls, where action three means roughly the same thing across very different generated environments, even though we never supervised what action three meant.

What's exciting to me is that this decoupling opens a path to learning from the huge amount of video on the internet without action labels. The model discovers a controllable interface on its own, and that could eventually be useful for training generalist agents.

r001.rationale: The response says the dynamics model predicts next-frame tokens, but does not state that the tokenizer’s decoder reconstructs an image from them.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the dynamics model predicts tokens for the next frame, distinguishing token prediction from generating the rendered frame itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, because I think people sometimes hear "world model" and assume it's just a video prediction model, and there's a bit more going on than that. The way I think about it is that there are really three pieces in Genie, and prediction is only one of them.

The first piece is a video tokenizer. We take the raw frames and compress them into discrete tokens, so instead of operating on pixels we're operating on a much smaller vocabulary of learned codes. That's just about representation, it's not making any predictions about the future.

The second piece, and this is the part I find most interesting, is the latent action model. We never had action labels. This was all trained on unlabeled internet video of people playing platformer games. So we needed some way to infer what happened between two frames. The latent action model looks at frame t and frame t plus one and tries to encode the difference into a very small discrete code, something like eight possible actions. We use a bottleneck there deliberately, because if you give it too much capacity it just memorizes the next frame and the "action" becomes meaningless. With a tight bottleneck, the only thing that survives is the controllable change, which turns out to look a lot like "move left," "move right," "jump."

Then the third piece is the dynamics model, and that's where the actual prediction lives. It takes the history of tokenized frames plus the latent action you selected and predicts the tokens for the next frame. So when you ask what Genie predicts versus how it generates, the distinction is that the dynamics model predicts in token space, conditioned on an action, and then generation is really just decoding those predicted tokens back to pixels through the tokenizer's decoder.

The nice property of splitting it that way is that at inference time you don't need the latent action model's encoder at all. The user just picks one of the discrete action codes, the dynamics model rolls forward, and you get a frame you can actually control. So prediction and generation are coupled, but the controllability comes from the action interface sitting in between them, not from the decoder itself.

r001.rationale: It says the tokenizer’s decoder turns the predicted tokens back into pixels.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes predicting next-frame tokens in token space from decoding those tokens into pixels.

astra-6.text: The distinction is between predicting the dynamics and decoding those predictions into pixels. Genie takes the previous frames and an action, and its dynamics model predicts tokens representing what should happen next. Then the video decoder turns those predicted tokens into the next frame. So when we say it predicts the next frame, it’s really predicting in a compressed representation; generating the image is the decoding step.

r001.rationale: It says the video decoder turns Genie’s predicted tokens into the next frame, conveying reconstruction of the image from those tokens.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes the dynamics model predicting tokens in a compressed representation from decoding those tokens into the frame.

sol-6.1.text:
The distinction is between predicting the action and predicting what happens as a result of that action. During training, Genie’s latent action model looks at two consecutive frames and learns a compact representation of the change between them. We don’t have action labels, so it isn’t told, “That was a jump” or “That was moving left.” It discovers those distinctions from the video.

The dynamics model then takes the previous frames and that latent action and predicts the next frame in a compressed token representation, which is decoded back into an image. At generation time, the user chooses a latent action, and the dynamics model generates what comes next. So the action model learns a control signal, and the dynamics model learns its consequences.

r001.rationale: The response says the compressed token representation is decoded into an image, but does not identify the decoder as the tokenizer’s decoder.

r002.rationale: It states that the dynamics model predicts the next frame in a compressed token representation, which is then decoded into an image, distinguishing token prediction from direct image prediction.
